aim: To investigate the effects of listening to modern music, categorized as stimulative or sedative, on EEG patterns, BP, HR, and Resp.
findings_summary: A transient decrease in right and left parietal Theta and Alpha was observed when both music types began; this activity then increased 2 min into the music. Theta increase to stimulative music was brief, to sedative music left maintained a high level throughout the music and right began to decrease after 3 mins. Alpha increased to stimulative but not sedative music. HR increased a little to stimulative music but not to sedative music. BP decreased during both stimulative and sedative music (both systolic and diastolic). Resp increased to stimulative but not sedative music.

stimulus.source: Every Little Time from Eurobeat and Song for Peace composed by Kitaro and played on a synthesizer.

design.control_baseline: Before: 7 min (first 2 min excluded) rest; After: 5 min rest

findings.eeg: Transient ↓ right & left parietal theta and alpha at music onset; ↑ after 2 min. Stimulative music: ↑ Theta (brief); ↑ Alpha. Sedative music: ↑ Theta (left parietal); ≈ Alpha.
findings.ecg: Stimulative music: slight ↑ HR; ↓ BP (both systolic and diastolic); ↑ Resp. Sedative music: ≈ HR; ↓ BP (both systolic and diastolic); ≈ Resp.

aim: Investigate old Japanese music using EEG, BP, HR and Resp.
findings_summary: Left and right parietal Theta and Alpha showed significant increases during listening, with sex differences. BP and HR decreased but Resp increased slightly during music.

stimulus.source: Gagaku, an old Japanese ceremonial music form.

design.control_baseline: Before: 7 min (first 2 min excluded) rest; After: 5 min rest.

findings.eeg: ↑ left & right parietal theta and alpha, with sex differences.

aim: To examine the influence of visual and musical stimuli on brain processing using classical musical excerpts to evoke the three basic emotions of happiness, sadness and fear.
findings_summary: Alpha power density was largest (reflecting reduced brain activity) for sound conditions, intermediate for picture conditions, and lowest for the combined presentations. HR and Resp increased significantly during conditions involving music compared to visual only.

participants.eligibility_criteria: Physical evaluation to screen out chronic diseases, mental disorders, medication, drug or alcohol abuse. Depression, anxiety and alexithymia were assessed with participants outside normal range excluded.

eeg.hardware: Easy Cap System, Brain Vision amplifier, recorder and analyzer

stimulus.source: Excerpts of exactly 70 s from: (1) Gustav Holst: Mars the Bringer of War from The Planets; (2) Samuel Barber, Adagio for Strings; and (3) Beethoven, Symphony no. 6 (3rd mvt).
stimulus.attention: Instructed to place themselves into the same mood as expressed by the stimuli.

design.hypothesis: That the combined presentation of two emotional stimuli will result in increased activation in emotional brain structures and correspondingly increase subjective and psychophysiological arousal
design.orientation: Seated (with head in a chin rest)
design.control_baseline: Compared music, music + visual, visual (no neutral control)

aim: To explicitly test the hypothesis that harmonic expectancy violations are also emotionally significant.
findings_summary: Very unexpected chord (Neapolitan Sixth) elicited a distinct early negativity (EN) (~230 ms). The EN was followed by a slight positivity. Unexpected chord elicited an EN ~310 msec broadly distributed over the scalp, strongest over fronto‐central sites.^b No significant changes in the IBI for the three different types of harmonization in any of the three time windows (0–2 s, 2–4 s, 4–6 s).

participants.musicianship: No musical training beyond classroom music at school^a

eeg.filtering: Filtered off‐line using a band‐pass filter with a frequency range of 0.25–25 Hz (3001 points, FIR)

stimulus.source: Three matched versions of six Bach chorales, differing only by one chord to be harmonically expected, unexpected, and very unexpected. Taken from previously recorded MIDI files and altered in CuBase SX. Played without expressive features, tempo and loudness kept constant throughout. Score cited. Pieces and sections used provided in a table. Score example in figure.
stimulus.attention: Compared length of extract and indicated if longer or shorter than previous.

design.hypothesis: That increasing harmonic unexpectedness would heighten subjective emotion, perceived tension, physiological arousal, and elicit specific brain responses.^a
design.control_baseline: EEG: averages computed with a 2500 ms prestimulus baseline^c, ECG: averages computed with a 1 s prestimulus baseline^c

findings.eeg: Very unexpected chord (Neapolitan Sixth) elicited distinct EN (~230 ms) followed by slight positivity. Unexpected chord elicited EN ~310 ms broadly distributed over the scalp, strongest over fronto‐central sites.

aim: To investigate ERPs and HR in response to unexpected chords (as composed by classical composers) in a condition in which musical excerpts were played with musical expression by a pianist, and a condition in which excerpts were played without musical expression by a computer (no variation in tempo or loudness).
findings_summary: Both unexpected and highly unexpected chords triggered an early right anterior negativity (ERAN), whose amplitude nominally varied with harmonic irregularity (non‐significant). Emotional expression influenced N5 amplitude, without significant P3a effects, suggesting music syntax and emotion processing are distinct. No significant differences in IBI across chord types or expressiveness levels.

participants.musicianship: No formal musical training besides normal school education

eeg.variables: Early right anterior negativity (ERAN) and the N5 ERPs
eeg.reference: Left mastoid as reference. Re‐referenced to the algebraic mean of the left and right mastoid.

stimulus.source: 25 excerpts from Sonatas by Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, and Schubert, played by professional pianists and recorded to MIDI to create three harmonic versions of each excerpt (Expected, Unexpected, and Very Unexpected) by modifying a single chord, resulting in 75 unique files. For each of those 75 files a non‐expressive version was created by digitally removing all tempo and loudness variation, resulting in 150 stimuli in total. Score example in figure.
stimulus.attention: Button press to indicate detection of chords played with a deviant instrument.

design.hypothesis: That unexpected harmonies, compared to expected, would increase both physiological arousal and specific neural responses. That musical expression would further increase physiological arousal but not influence brain responses.
design.control_baseline: EEG: 200‐ms prestimulus baseline for each ERP. ECG baseline not reported.^c

findings.eeg: Unexpected and highly unexpected chords triggered ERAN (amplitude ≈ varied with harmonic irregularity). Expression influenced N5 amplitude (↑ for expressive vs. unexpressive performance); ≈ P3a.

aim: To investigate the effects of musical stimuli commonly used in music therapy with other auditory stimuli on neurophysiological and behavioral responses in individuals with disorders of consciousness.^c
findings_summary: Liked music had greatest effect on right hemisphere EEG amplitude with similar increases to white noise in left. Distinct responses in frontal and temporal regions across bandwidths, with bias towards right hemisphere. Significant peak increase in Resp to liked music. Eyes Closed (EC) LF HRV approached significance, but change was non‐specific across stimuli. Significance for HR and HRV was less clearly defined in relation to effects of individual stimuli.^c

participants.musicianship: High level of musical proficiency excluded^b
participants.final_number_processed: EEG = 19 1 missing due to corrupted data^b
participants.age_years: Male^b 29–59 M = 41 SD = 11 Female 24–52 M = 34 SD = 12.5

eeg.filtering: Hi/low cut off bandpass filter at 0.5 and 30 Hz.
eeg.hardware: XLTEC 50 channel video EEG and neuro‐physiological acquisition system

ecg.recording_equipment: XLTEC 50 channel video EEG and neuro‐physiological acquisition system

stimulus.source: Digital recordings of disliked music and white noise.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator, participant selected from own collection

design.visual_state: EO, EC; only EC analyzed.^b “Instructed to close their eyes half way into each stimulus presentation to provide both eyes open and closed data” (p. 4).

findings.eeg: ↑ frontal right alpha and beta (liked music). ↑ frontal‐midline theta for liked vs. disliked music.
findings.ecg: ↑ Peak Resp (liked music). ≈ HRV, although increase in eyes‐closed LF HRV was near‐significant (p = 0.054).

aim: To investigate the effects, and their time course, of inaudible high‐frequency components in high‐resolution music on EEG and HR.
findings_summary: High‐alpha EEG power significantly higher for full‐range music excerpts compared to high‐cut ones at left occipital region during last 50 s of listening, indicating a brain response to high‐frequency components without conscious awareness or changes in subjective feelings, heart rate, or facial expressions. No significant main or interaction effects of sound type for HR.

participants.eligibility_criteria: Self‐reported normal hearing and vision and no history of neurological disorders

eeg.reference: Average reference online; re‐referenced to the linked‐earlobe reference (A1, A2) offline.

stimulus.source: First 200 s of French Suite No. 5 by J. S. Bach played on cembalo (harpsichord), and a high‐cut version produced by digitally removing all frequencies above 20 kHz using a specialized low‐pass filter with an extremely steep slope (−1673 dB/octave). Supporting Information shows average power spectra of the two versions of the music.
stimulus.attention: Asked to listen to the music.

design.visual_state: EO—while looking at a landscape picture

findings.eeg: ↑ High‐alpha power in left occipital region during last 50 s (full‐range vs. high‐cut music).

aim: To identify EEG oscillation time course patterns, and psychophysiological arousal, related to musical stimulus acoustic features and assess their stability during repeated exposure to the same piece of music.
findings_summary: Continuous increase in Event Related Synchronization in all frequency bands during music listening (relative to the pre‐music baseline). HR consistent across presentations. HR was lower in minute 2 of the 3‐min listening period. HR decreased with increased acoustic complexity and event‐related synchronization, despite an increase in EEG relative power and event‐related synchronization in central and parietal areas during listening.

participants.musicianship: No history of musical training, as assessed by an in‐house questionnaire
participants.eligibility_criteria: No reported history of present or past neurological, psychiatric, or audiological disorders. Participants denied consuming illegal drugs or regular medication
participants.age_years: Male M = 23.5 SD = 2.8 Female M = 22.2 SD = 8.7 Combined M = 22.53 SD = 7.47

eeg.reference: Cz served as an on‐line reference
eeg.filtering: Band‐pass filtered at 0.1–100 Hz. band‐pass filtered (1–40 Hz) including a notch‐filter of 50 Hz.

stimulus.source: iTunes version of Nessun dorma, as sung by Paul Potts (~175 s duration).
stimulus.attention: Instructed to listen carefully to the music.

design.control_baseline: 5 s baseline immediately before music presentation

findings.eeg: ↑ Theta, low alpha‐1, low alpha‐2, upper alpha, and beta power (i.e., continuous ↑ event‐related synchronization). Positive correlations between acoustic variables (acoustic envelope, acoustic complexity) and power synchronization in each band.
findings.ecg: ↓ HR in minute 2 (of 3 min listening). Negative correlation between acoustic complexity and HR.
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: Negative correlation between HR and the event‐related synchronization in each band across the time course of music listening.

aim: To investigate the effects of tempo and cognition in music listening on eigen decomposition of cardiac‐synchronized EEG.
findings_summary: Eigen values decreased while listening to music, most significantly to slow song and particularly at P3. T4 showed the greatest change in EEG dimensionality: most concentrated variance during slow song, most distributed during favorite song. ECG measures were not reported.

eeg.variables: Amplitude eigenvalues 300 ms pre R peak

stimulus.source: Slow & fast tempo songs, favorite song which “moved” them.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from own collection

findings.eeg: ↓ Eigenvalues; slow song produced most significant decreases (T3, T4, P3). P3 most sensitive across all songs. T4 showed the greatest change in EEG dimensionality: most concentrated variance during slow song, most distributed during favorite song.

aim: To investigate the effects of tempo and cognition induced by auditory stimuli using cardiac‐synchronized EEG segments
findings_summary: Parietal Alpha most sensitive to auditory input. Gamma (right hemisphere) most sensitive to cognition. Favorite song caused largest changes in all EEG. Fast tempo song caused larger changes than slow. Alpha, Gamma and Gamma2 significantly affected by auditory input; Theta, least affected; Delta, no significant changes. ECG measures were not reported (Cognitive engagement was operationalized as a self‐selected favorite vs. an unfamiliar song).

eeg.variables: Eigen decomposition of the covariance of the data matrix of pre R peak EEG segments

stimulus.source: Slow & fast tempo songs, favorite song. Local phase randomized favorite and fast tempo songs.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from own collection

design.hypothesis: That interactions between cardio‐cerebral rhythms cause changes in neuronal oscillations when auditory stimuli are synchronized with cardiac rhythm.

findings.eeg: Parietal alpha most sensitive to auditory input. Gamma (right hemisphere) most sensitive to cognition. Favorite song caused largest changes. Alpha, Gamma & Gamma2 significantly affected; Theta least affected; Delta no significant changes.

aim: To investigate the synchronization of autonomic and cerebral rhythms by music, specifically focusing on how tempo and familiarity of songs influence physiological responses.
findings_summary: Increase in coherence, indicating degree of synchronization, among cerebral, cardiovascular and respiratory rhythms during music listening. All songs significantly increased cerebro‐RR coherencies in the HF and LF band, slow tempo songs produced higher increases than fast tempo and larger effect sizes in frontal lobe and right hemisphere.

participants.eligibility_criteria: Exclusion: age < 18 years or > 37 years, pregnancy; hypertension; history of epilepsy or seizures; photosensitivity; adverse reaction after listening to certain music, songs or sounds; psychotropic drug use that could affect alertness or cognitive functions

eeg.variables: LF and HF coherence of EEG with RR, SBP, DBP, and Respiration.
eeg.filtering: The envelope function in MATLAB was used to compute the envelopes of the EEG. The envelopes, respiration and piecewise constant HR, SBP, and DBP were low‐pass filtered with a cutoff frequency of 5 Hz and sub‐sampled at a rate of 10 samples/s.

ecg.filtering: Low‐pass filtered with a cutoff frequency of 5 Hz and sub‐sampled at a rate of 10 samples/s.

stimulus.source: Favorite song. Fast and slow tempo vocal songs in Italian language. Favorite song and unknown (fast) songs processed for local phase randomization.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from own collection

design.control_baseline: 10 min, no music & no headphone over ears, before and after

findings.eeg: ↑ coherence of EEG with cardiovascular and respiratory rhythms (see EEG‐ECG).
findings.ecg: HR and IBI reported as part of coherence analysis (see EEG‐ECG).
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: ↑ coherence among cerebral, cardiovascular & respiratory rhythms during music listening. Slow tempo songs ↑ higher than fast; larger effect sizes in frontal region & right hemisphere.

aim: To investigate the relationship between scaling behavior in music and cortical dynamics in mediating music listening pleasure. Characterized the self‐similarity of fluctuations in loudness, pitch, and rhythm of 12 classical pieces and analyzed the scaling behavior of multiscale neuronal activity from different scalp regions and cardiac IBIs at baseline and during music listening, and associated these with self‐reported pleasure.
findings_summary: Implicated alpha, beta and gamma bands in music processing. Neuronal and cardiac dynamics showed a significant positive correlation during music listening. Music listening decreased the neuronal scaling exponent in temporal areas, linked to pleasure. Higher default‐state scaling exponents in pleased individuals were higher and approached those found in music loudness fluctuations. HR (AVNN) increased during music and was proportional to pitch scaling. Standard HRV measures were modulated by music, but α₁ (heart) was not consistently affected.

participants.musicianship: Were not musicians; only roughly half had any formal music training
participants.eligibility_criteria: No history of neurological disease or psychiatric disorders

eeg.variables: Scaling exponent of neuronal activity in various frequency bands
eeg.filtering: Non‐notch sinusoidal removal (PREP pipeline). Avoided standard high‐pass/notch filters to minimize long‐term signal distortion and preserve high‐frequency activity. Used a small sliding window (< 1 s) (Bigdely‐Shamlo et al. 2015)

ecg.variables: HRV measures including time‐domain (AVNN, SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50), frequency‐domain (VLF, LF, HF, and LF/HF), and α₁ (heart)
ecg.filtering: A low‐pass filter (cut‐off frequency: 100 Hz) and a notch filter (~50 Hz) were applied during recording. After acquisition, high‐pass and low‐pass two‐way constrained least squares FIR filters (cutoff 45 Hz, order = 500; cutoff 0.5 Hz, order = 1200, −70 dB stopband attenuation, passband ripple = 0.1%) were used to eliminate baseline drift of non‐cardiac origin and minimize other artifacts such as power line interference or electromyographic noise.

stimulus.style: Classical Piano compositions from the Humdrum Kern database
stimulus.source: Two distinct compositions from six different composers obtained from Qobuz.com. Details of composer, performer and piece provided in Supporting Information the paper.
stimulus.attention: Visual cue before each piece signaling to concentrate on the music.

design.hypothesis: That the brain's sensitivity and pleasure from music arise from the shared dynamical patterns between the music's scaling and the brain's neuronal scaling behavior.

findings.eeg: Alpha, beta & gamma bands implicated in music processing. Neuronal scaling exponent ↓ in temporal areas, linked to pleasure.
findings.ecg: ↑ HR (AVNN), proportional to pitch scaling. HRV measures modulated but α₁ (heart) not consistently affected.
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: Positive correlation between neuronal & cardiac dynamics during music listening.

aim: To measure changes in neuronal communication during music listening, using coherence, and to explore if any physiological variables including HR, BP, respiration and brain electrical responses became synchronized with songs.
findings_summary: Music listening increases synchronization among low‐frequency brain responses and physiological variables. Slow songs showed the highest, and fast songs the lowest, synchronization, with T4 showing the greatest synchronization, and the right hemisphere exhibiting larger average coherence compared to the left.

eeg.variables: MSC of low frequency time series extracted from envelope profile of EEG

ecg.filtering: Low passed filtered by a cutoff frequency of 5 Hz and down‐sampled to rate of 10 samples/s.

stimulus.source: Slow & fast tempo songs. Two songs, known and unknown, and two scrambled phase of local spectra versions of known and unknown songs.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from own collection

findings.eeg: ↑ synchronization among low‐frequency brain responses and physiological variables (see EEG‐ECG).
findings.ecg: IBI reported as part of coherence analysis (see EEG‐ECG).
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: ↑ synchronization among low‐frequency brain responses & physiological variables. Slow songs highest, fast lowest. T4 greatest synchronization; right hemisphere>left.

aim: To investigate the synchronization of the brain and heart responses to different auditory stimuli using complexity‐based analysis (fractal dimensions and sample entropy).
findings_summary: EEG complexity increases with music complexity, showing a strong correlation, while HRV complexity decreases in response to music, with both EEG and HRV complexity synchronizing to music's fractal dimension, indicating a unified response of brain and heart to musical complexity.

participants.eligibility_criteria: Did not drink alcohol/caffeine before the experiment

eeg.variables: Fractal dimension and sample entropy of EEG
eeg.filtering: Removed DC offset then a fourth‐order Butterworth band‐pass filter (1–40 Hz)

stimulus.source: Für Elise by Beethoven, altered by white, pink & brown noise.^a

findings.eeg: EEG complexity ↑ with music complexity, showing strong correlation.
findings.ecg: HRV complexity ↓ in response to music though not statistically significant.
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: Both EEG & HRV complexity synchronized to music's fractal dimension, indicating unified brain‐heart response.

aim: To investigate the effects of listening to music on EEG segments synchronized to different phases of the cardiac cycle, specifically focusing on how the tempo and cognition of music influence the complexity of brain responses in different brain regions.
findings_summary: Complexity of EEG responses increased with tempo and cognitive engagement, particularly for fast and favorite songs, with parietal and temporal lobes most affected; slow songs had a less complex, calming effect, indicating tempo and cognition have distinct impacts on brain activity, with cognition eliciting higher frequency responses and tempo affecting lower frequencies. ECG measures were not reported.

eeg.variables: Eigen decomposition of autocovariance of EEG segments synchronized to three different 300 ms segments of the cardiac cycle
eeg.filtering: Bandpass Butterworth IIR filter. In total band, no bandpass filter was used, and 0.5–100 Hz and 0.5–125 Hz bands (filtered by the same bandpass Butterworth) were used to confirm the results of the total band.

stimulus.source: Slow and fast tempo songs. An unknown (fast) song and favorite song. Phase randomized version of known and unknown songs.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from own collection

findings.eeg: Complexity of EEG ↑ with tempo & cognitive engagement, particularly for fast & favorite songs. Parietal & temporal lobes most affected; slow songs less complex; right hemisphere>left.

aim: To investigate coupling between EEG and ECG to changes in music complexity using SE of EEG and HRV.
findings_summary: Lower fractal complexity of the music stimulus led to greater change in EEG and HRV Shannon entropy. Music, EEG and HRV SE changes correlated. SE of EEG lowest at rest. Increased with each music presentation. Brown noise shows largest difference. EEG variations significant. HRV inverse of EEG: SE of HRV highest during rest and reduced with each music presentation. HRV variations not significant.

participants.eligibility_criteria: Had a “complete health condition” and did not drink alcohol/caffeine for 24 h before experiments

eeg.reference: 3 reference electrodes as shown in (Liu et al. 2020), fig.1
eeg.filtering: Removed DC offset then a fourth‐order Butterworth band‐pass filter (1–40 Hz)

stimulus.source: Für Elise by Beethoven, rhythm complexity altered by white, pink & brown noise.^a

findings.eeg: SE of EEG lowest at rest; ↑ with each music presentation. Brown noise (lowest complexity) music showed largest difference from rest.
findings.ecg: SE of HRV highest during rest; ↓ with each music presentation (inverse of EEG). HRV variations not significant.
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: Music, EEG & HRV SE changes correlated.

aim: To examine the anxiolytic effect of incremental modulations in tempo and octave.
findings_summary: Significant decrease in lower frequency EEG power in bilateral temporo‐parieto‐occipital regions compared to those who listened to SM or silence. SM group exhibited increase in higher frequencies, suggesting a different pattern of brain activity compared to the VM group. Significant decrease in HRV based on relative R‐R intervals for silence but not during music. No significant difference in other HRV parameters.

stimulus.source: Two custom recorded instrumental pieces played on Violin and Mridangam, one with incremental variations in tempo and octave. Details in text in Supporting Information of the paper.

design.hypothesis: That music with incremental tempo and octave modulations would produce a greater anxiolytic (anxiety‐reducing) physiological and psychological response compared to music without these changes or silence.
design.time_of_day: Morning, Noon and Evening sessions (3 pm—7 pm)
design.control_baseline: EEG analysis: 3 min silent rest (baseline) before intervention; and during 8 min intervention (stable/variable music vs. silence [control]) ECG: ‘resting state’ activity on the first vs. last day of each 1‐week intervention (music, silence). Note: Intervention involved 6 sessions over 1 week. See paper for full timing details.

findings.eeg: Significant ↓ lower frequency EEG power in bilateral temporo‐parieto‐occipital regions for VM. SM group ↑ in higher frequencies.
findings.ecg: Significant ↓ rrHRV for silence but not during music. No significant difference in other HRV parameters.

aim: To investigate the brain‐heart interplay that is consistently observed across different mental states (music listening and rest).
findings_summary: A positive association between parieto‐occipital alpha2 power (10–12 Hz) in EEG and nHF, during both music listening and rest. This relationship persisted even after accounting for other variables such as mental fatigue, sleepiness, and emotional arousal, suggesting a robust brain‐heart interaction across different mental states.

eeg.filtering: Offline bandpass filter from 2 to 40 Hz
eeg.hardware: 8 channel Neuroelectrics cap. StarStim (Neuroelectrics, Barcelona, Spain)

stimulus.source: 8 Pieces from the Music Emotion Recognition (MER) database plus 4 that were familiar and likely to evoke emotion.
stimulus.selection: Pre‐selected by investigator; participant selected from a limited set

findings.eeg: Parieto‐occipital alpha2 power (10–12 Hz) assessed (see EEG‐ECG).
findings.eeg_ecg_interaction: Positive partial correlation between parieto‐occipital alpha2 power & nHF during both music listening (accounting for arousal & valence) & rest (accounting for fatigue & sleepiness).
